claims.text: An active-learning machine-learning-potential and reweighting method can accurately compute solid and liquid free-energy surfaces near melting.
The computed free energies can retain vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
Suitable ab initio molecular-dynamics and TOR-TILD reference results exist for elemental and binary metals near melting.
A machine-learning force-field surrogate can be trained using a sparse set of ab initio molecular-dynamics snapshots.
Active learning can iteratively identify and add the ab initio configurations needed to maintain surrogate accuracy.
Reweighting with the surrogate can obtain solid and liquid free energies using substantially fewer expensive ab initio MD steps.
Force-field simulations can reproduce selected first-principles and experimental properties of a multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
Agreement of a force-field model with selected HEA structural, stability, ordering, and mechanical properties supports accurate free-energy mapping near fusion.
The surrogate can accurately reproduce complex interactions including electron–vibration coupling.
The surrogate and reweighting workflow can bypass long explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics trajectories.
The proposed method should match explicit ab initio MD within a few kJ/mol in free energy or approximately ±50 K in melting temperature.
The proposed method should reduce computational time by one to two orders of magnitude relative to full ab initio MD.
The proposed method should maintain higher throughput than TOR-TILD for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
TOR-TILD is effective for elemental and binary systems but becomes inefficient for high-entropy alloys.
The method is expected to apply near melting in elemental and binary metallic systems and may extend to multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Performance may be limited in systems with especially delicate electron–vibration coupling or poor cross-phase transferability.
The method can be benchmarked by comparing solid–liquid free-energy differences, melting temperature, latent heat, statistical error, and convergence against explicit ab initio MD.
A free-energy error above a few kJ/mol or a melting-temperature deviation above ±50 K constitutes falsification.
